correctness.rationale: Every nonempty proper induced cycle subgraph is a path forest. Cyclic positive-run compositions count its component-size partition exactly; its isomorphism-group order is \(\prod_{j}m_j!\,2^{r-m_1}\). Thus the sum of two independent domain/image counts times this order is exact, with separate empty and dihedral cases. For any rank k, r<=min(k,n-k); a single independent set has floor(n/2)! automorphisms, bounding the full monoid between factorial and \(4^n2^ss!\). Stirling proves the leading logarithmic growth and tail bound. Partitions of fixed deficiency prove the high-rank asymptotic, and {0,2}->{0,3} distinguishes adjacency from ambient distances. Direct independent finite bijection enumeration verified all coefficients for n=3,...,9, but is not used to infer the all-n results.

originality.rationale: Best-knowledge novelty: the inspected 2018 general graph-monoid paper establishes the ambient object but not a cycle rank count; the 2021 path theorem concerns open chains; the 2022 cycle-isometry theorem counts only the much smaller ambient-distance-preserving submonoid; the 2022 crown-poset theorem concerns a different relational signature and generating rank. Neither these statements nor checked accessible prior claim titles/claims imply the closed cyclic-run formula, fixed-deficiency leading term, or quantitative half-rank concentration. A hidden stronger implication remains a residual risk, so this is not a global priority certificate.

value.rationale: The complete rank enumerator is a canonical structural invariant of the induced-graph partial-automorphism inverse monoid of a cycle, with a uniform proof for every n. Its half-rank concentration, superexponential macroscopic tail decay, and n log n cardinality scale characterize qualitatively different behavior from the well-studied smaller cycle partial-isometry monoid. A fixed-deficiency law describes the opposite end of the rank spectrum. These statements motivate and refine general inverse-semigroup and graph-automorphism enumeration beyond a routine small finite case.
